title: What if you could see like a bee?

narration.heading: Bee vision
narration.text: You wake up, and every flower in the garden has a secret pattern on it.

narration.heading: What you see
narration.text: Your eyes see light from about three hundred and eighty to seven hundred and fifty nanometres. That's every rainbow you've ever seen.

narration.heading: What bees see
narration.text: But bees see something you can't: ultraviolet, just past violet. And they can't see red at all.

narration.heading: How seeing works
narration.text: So how would that work for you? Light enters your eye, your lens filters it, and your retina reads it.

narration.heading: The catch
narration.text: Here's the catch. Your cones can already sense a little ultraviolet. It's your lens that blocks it.

narration.heading: UV vision
narration.text: Without it, plain yellow flowers suddenly show dark bullseyes. Patterns painted there to guide bees to the nectar.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: The twist? This really happened. In nineteen twenty-three, the painter Claude Monet had a cataract removed, and lost that lens.

narration.heading: Monet's lilies
narration.text: Afterwards, his water lilies turned blue and purple. Some scientists think he was painting light you can't see.

narration.heading: Your call
narration.text: So would you trade seeing red for seeing ultraviolet?

skit.text: Ultraviolet? Please. I only see in dark mode.

titles: What if you could see like a bee?
Your eyes can almost see ultraviolet. Here's what stops them
youtube.description: Bees see ultraviolet patterns on flowers that are invisible to us, and the only thing stopping your eyes is your lens. Even Monet may have painted it.

sources.claim: A typical human eye responds to wavelengths from about 380 to about 750 nanometres
Bees and many other insects can detect ultraviolet light; bees' long-wavelength cutoff is about 590 nm, short of red
Our lenses filter out UV light; human cones can perceive UV if given the chance
In some plants, such as the meadow buttercup, nectar guides are visible only in ultraviolet light, attracting pollinators such as honey bees
People without a lens perceive ultraviolet light as whitish blue or whitish violet
Monet's cataract surgery took place in January 1923; his later water lilies gained blue and purple overtones, which some link to seeing UV
